Baby & Child

Lissencephaly: diagnosis, development and care

Updated: October 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Lissencephaly describes an uncommon difference in brain development in which the outer brain layer has fewer folds than expected. It is a structural condition present from early development, not a diagnosis made from head shape alone. Its cause, extent and effects vary; a single lifespan or developmental limit cannot describe every child.

What a smoother brain surface means

Normally, nerve cells move into organised layers as the fetal brain develops, and the cortex forms ridges and grooves. In classic lissencephaly, disrupted development produces absent folds, called agyria, or unusually broad ridges, called pachygyria. Pachygyria does not mean simply thickened grooves.

The pattern may involve much of the brain or only part of it. Different causes can affect other brain structures and organs. Imaging terminology and severity descriptions help specialists explain findings, but a grade alone cannot predict a child’s future abilities.

Symptoms and development are individual

Possible features include delayed head control or movement, learning and communication difficulties, low muscle tone that may later become stiffness, seizures and problems feeding or swallowing. Some children have a small head, either at birth or as they grow; this is not required for the diagnosis.

Hand, finger or toe differences can occur with some associated syndromes, rather than in every child. Vision, hearing, growth and motor skills also deserve assessment. Skills and support needs vary with the underlying condition; do not assume that all children stop developing at three to five months.

Can it be recognised during pregnancy?

Specialist ultrasound may raise concern, with fetal MRI sometimes adding information about the cortex or associated findings. A fetal brain normally has fewer visible folds earlier in pregnancy. A normal early scan therefore cannot exclude lissencephaly, and there is no universal week-20 or week-23 diagnostic rule.

MRI is an additional specialist test, not a routine requirement for every pregnancy. Later assessment may show cortical development more clearly, with timing based on the clinical question. A family history or known genetic variant warrants genetic counselling; targeted prenatal testing may be possible, but results and imaging cannot always predict severity.

Causes and related conditions need careful distinction

Many forms have a genetic cause, including changes affecting PAFAH1B1 or DCX. A change may arise newly or be inherited, depending on the condition. Nerve-cell migration is a complex developmental process, not a single event confined to weeks 12–14 in which every affected cell simply stays still.

Lissencephaly can occur on its own or in a syndrome. Miller–Dieker syndrome involves a chromosome deletion and additional features. Walker–Warburg syndrome is a distinct brain, muscle and eye disorder with a cobblestone cortical pattern; it should not be treated as identical to classic lissencephaly. Possible infection or vascular injury requires its own assessment, not an assumed explanation or parental blame.

How diagnosis is established after birth

A paediatric neurology team combines the child’s history, examination and development with brain imaging, usually MRI to characterise the cortex. Ultrasound or CT may be useful in particular circumstances, but not every child needs all three. EEG assesses suspected seizures; it does not replace structural imaging.

Genetic testing is selected with counselling, sometimes including chromosome or broader gene testing. It can clarify the cause and family recurrence risk, although not every test finds an answer. The extent of agyria or pachygyria, associated changes and the clinical course matter more than assuming that most children share one grade or prognosis.

Treatment supports health and participation

No current treatment restores normal cortical folding, but active care can improve comfort, safety and participation. Seizure treatment is tailored by specialists to the seizure type and response. Physiotherapy, occupational therapy, communication support and help with stiffness or positioning are adapted to the child’s goals.

Swallowing assessment, nutrition and respiratory care are important when feeding is difficult or food enters the airway. Some children need temporary tube feeding or a gastrostomy, chosen with the family rather than automatically. Monitor growth, constipation, vision and hearing. Enlarged brain fluid spaces do not by themselves mandate surgery; confirmed hydrocephalus needs specialist assessment and sometimes a drainage procedure.

When to seek urgent help

Call emergency services for a first suspected seizure, even if it has stopped, a seizure lasting longer than usual or more than five minutes when the usual duration is unknown, repeated seizures without recovery, or three or more seizures in 24 hours. Also get immediate emergency help for breathing difficulty, blue or grey lips or tongue, fainting or loss of consciousness or inability to wake the child. Do not wait five minutes with breathing trouble.

For known epilepsy, follow the trained, individual emergency plan. New clusters of brief bending or jerking movements may be infantile spasms and need urgent assessment that day; NICE calls for specialist guidance and referral within 24 hours for suspected spasms under age two. New feeding deterioration, choking, reduced urine, repeated vomiting or a bulging soft spot also needs prompt urgent advice; severe illness or reduced responsiveness is an emergency.

Prognosis is not one number

Some children have profound disability and difficult-to-control epilepsy; others achieve more motor or communication skills. Aspiration, respiratory illness and severe seizures can shorten life, but a ten-year lifespan or a three-to-five-month developmental ceiling must not be applied to all lissencephaly. Some affected people live into adulthood.

A 2026 study found different developmental patterns across genetic groups, but its selected cohort cannot predict an individual child’s outcome. More limited changes can have milder effects without guaranteeing near-normal development. Discuss the child’s own progress and complications with the team, revisiting goals as needs change.

Planning care with the family

Ask for a coordinated plan covering seizures and rescue treatment, safe feeding, respiratory symptoms, therapies, equipment, follow-up and who to contact outside clinic hours. Families may need practical assistance, respite and emotional support alongside medical care. Comfort-focused support can accompany active treatment.

Genetic counselling can explain which tests are informative and whether relatives or a future pregnancy need assessment. Inheritance differs between causes, so a single recurrence percentage is misleading. Decisions should respect the child’s needs and the family’s preferences, without promising a cure or reducing the child to a scan result.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Ask the specialist to explain the cortical pattern, the suspected or confirmed genetic cause and what further imaging or testing could clarify. A normal early scan does not exclude every form, and a grade alone cannot predict development.

Keep an individual plan for seizures and rescue treatment, safe swallowing and nutrition, breathing care and developmental therapies. Do not change seizure medicines without the team’s advice, and do not continue feeding through choking.

Ask about cause-specific genetic counselling, future pregnancies and practical family support. Keep agreed follow-up, report new symptoms promptly and seek urgent care before recording them in an app.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help organise questions, appointments and observations for the care team. It cannot interpret a brain scan, diagnose a seizure, predict survival or replace genetic counselling. Do not let recording symptoms delay urgent care.

When to seek help

A first suspected seizure, even if it has stopped, or prolonged concerning seizures, repeated seizures without recovery, breathing difficulty, blue or grey lips or tongue, fainting or loss of consciousness or inability to wake require immediate emergency help. New suspected infantile spasms need urgent same-day assessment. Do not change seizure medicines, feed through choking or attempt treatment without the child’s clinical plan.

Evidence notes updated: October 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Lissencephaly involves reduced cortical folding; its cause and effects vary.
  • Normal early prenatal imaging cannot rule it out, and specialist testing has limits.
  • Seizure, swallowing, nutrition and developmental care are individual and active.
  • Breathing difficulty, inability to wake or concerning seizures need immediate emergency help; suspected infantile spasms need urgent assessment.
  • Neither lifespan nor future abilities can be predicted by one universal number.

Frequently asked questions

What causes lissencephaly?

Many forms result from genetic changes affecting brain development. Some arise newly and others are inherited. Related syndromes and other suspected causes need specific assessment; it is not evidence that a parent caused the condition.

Can a normal pregnancy scan exclude it?

No. Brain folds develop with gestation, and an early normal scan may not show a cortical difference. Specialist ultrasound, appropriately timed MRI and selected genetic testing may help, but no single scan or fixed week excludes every form.

How is it diagnosed after birth?

Clinical assessment and usually brain MRI establish the structural pattern. EEG helps investigate seizures, and selected genetic testing may identify the cause. Not every child needs ultrasound, CT and MRI together.

Can treatment reverse the brain changes?

Current care cannot restore normal folding, but it can address seizures, swallowing, nutrition, breathing, stiffness and communication. Therapies and feeding support are chosen for the child rather than a universal regimen.

Will the child develop or live only ten years?

There is no single developmental ceiling or lifespan for every form. Severe conditions may shorten life, while other people live into adulthood and achieve different skills. The cause, extent and complications guide individual counselling.

Does every child need a feeding tube or surgery?

No. Swallowing safety, growth and family circumstances guide feeding support. Some need a tube or gastrostomy. Hydrocephalus sometimes needs drainage, but enlarged fluid spaces alone do not automatically require surgery.

When are seizures an emergency?

A first suspected seizure, even if it has stopped, longer-than-usual event, over five minutes if usual duration is unknown, repeated events without recovery or three or more in 24 hours require emergency help. Breathing trouble, blue/grey lips or inability to wake require immediate help without waiting. Follow an established trained care plan for known epilepsy.

What about brief repeated jerks in a baby?

New clusters of bending or jerking may be infantile spasms, even when each is brief. Seek urgent assessment that day rather than waiting for a routine visit. If breathing, colour or responsiveness is affected, or emergency seizure signs occur, call emergency services immediately.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
